subject: Cloud Computing
title: Monolith vs. Distributed Systems
description: A quick win: understand Monolith vs. Distributed Systems.

hook.text: A single application handles everything: users, payments, emails. One bug crashes it all. That's a monolith.

buildup.text: Distributed systems split work across many services. Each runs independently and communicates over the network.

discovery.text: Monoliths are simple to build and deploy. Distributed systems are flexible but far more complex to manage.

twist.text: Many teams split monoliths too early. The complexity of distributed systems outweighs the benefits at small scale.

climax.text: The best approach: start monolith, split later when specific pain points emerge. Don't distribute for its own sake.

punchline.text: Monoliths aren't bad. Premature distribution is worse.

quiz.question: When should a team typically move from a monolith to distributed services?
options: When specific pain points emerge that distribution would solve
As soon as the first line of code is written
Only after the company has more than 1,000 employees

details.summary: A monolith packages all application logic into a single deployable unit, while distributed systems split logic across multiple networked services. Monoliths are simpler to develop and deploy but harder to scale selectively.
details.whyItMatters: Choosing between monolith and distributed architecture is one of the most consequential decisions in cloud engineering. The wrong choice creates years of technical debt.
takeaways: Monoliths are simpler to build, test, and deploy initially
Distributed systems allow independent scaling of components
Many teams start monolith and migrate to services later

faq.question: Is a monolith always bad for cloud deployments?
faq.answer: No. Monoliths are perfectly appropriate for small teams, early-stage products, and applications without extreme scaling needs. Many successful companies run monoliths in the cloud. Premature decomposition into microservices often creates more problems than it solves.

faq.question: How do you migrate from monolith to microservices?
faq.answer: The strangler fig pattern is the most common approach: incrementally extract functionality into new services while routing traffic away from the monolith. This avoids a risky big-bang rewrite and allows gradual validation of the new architecture.
